page_title: Seven habits of effective text editing

sources.entry: Bram Moolenaar (Vim author), Seven habits of effective text editing (presentation). This is about Vim but it contains good lessons about why investing time in learning how to be productive with your text editors pays off.

summary.title: Seven habits of effective text editing
summary.one_liner: Learn how to move, repeat, correct, and combine editing commands in Vim (with ideas that carry over to other editors) by spotting repetitive actions and training a few commands until they become habit.
keywords: unix filter text through external program
takeaways: Pick the few editor commands that speed up your own repeated actions, using a three-step loop: notice, look up, train.
Use search aids (*, incsearch, hlsearch), brace matching (%), and tags (CTRL-]) to move through code quickly.
Reduce retyping with the dot command, macros (qa ... q, @a), completion (CTRL-N), and abbreviations.
Use syntax highlighting to spot errors like unbalanced braces or misspelled directives, and use :make and :grep across project files.
Build habits gradually; learning touch typing and a small set of commands pays off over time.
summary.summary: Bram Moolenaar, the author of Vim, presents guidelines for faster, less error-prone editing of plain text and code. The paper is organised into seven sections: fast navigation, avoiding retyping, correcting mistakes, working across multiple files, integrating with external programs, handling structured text, and making good commands into habits. Each section gives concrete Vim commands and examples, and the examples are framed as a general method that applies to other editors. The paper concludes that you should learn only the 10 to 20 percent of commands you actually need and practise them until they are automatic.
